INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE 1
Amicus Curiae  Americans Against Gun Violence
(“AAGunV”) is a nonprofit organization founded in the
belief that the people of the United States have not only
the ability, but also the moral obligation to reduce rates
of firearm-related deaths and injuries in our country
to levels comparable to the rates in the other high
income democratic countries. In order to help fulfill this
obligation, AAGunV engages in educating the public
and policymakers regarding the causes of our country’s
extraordinarily high rate of firearm-related deaths and
injuries and the definitive measures needed to stop this
epidemic.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Petitioners rest their argument that the Second
Amendment guarantees a right to possess AR-15 platform
and similar semiautomatic rifles (“AR-15’s) entirely
upon this Court’s decision in District of Columbia v.
Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008)  and its progeny – not on the
history and text of the Second Amendment itself. Heller
and its progeny are egregiously flawed decisions that
are themselves incompatible with the history and plain
language of the Second Amendment, and these decisions
have devastating public health consequences. A ruling by
this Court in favor of Petitioners in the present case would
compound those devastating consequences.
1.  No party’s counsel authored this brief in whole or in part
and no party or party’s counsel made any monetary contribution
intended to fund the preparation or submission of this brief.

2
We call on this Court to rule not only that civilian
ownership of AR-15’s is not constitutionally protected, but
also to acknowledge Heller and its progeny were wrongly
decided.
ARGUMENT
I. Heller Was Wrongly Decided.
In Heller, a narrow five-justice majority reversed over
two centuries of legal precedent by ruling for the first
time that the Second Amendment conferred an individual
right to firearm ownership unrelated to service in a “well
regulated Milita.” Heller, 554 U.S. at 576-626; U.S. Const.,
amend. II.
The late Justice John Paul Stevens, having served 35
years on this Court and dissented in Heller, disagreed. In
his autobiography, Stevens wrote, “Heller is unquestionably
the most clearly incorrect decision that the Court
announced during my tenure on the bench.” John Paul
Stevens, The Making of a Justice: Reflections on My
First 94 Years, 482 (New York, Little Brown & Co. 2019).
Below we address the primary reasons why Heller was
wrongly decided and should be overturned by this Court.
A. Heller is incompatible with the “well regulated
Militia” clause of the Second Amendment.
Heller’s holding rested in part on an incompatible
reading of the text and purpose. As the Professors of
Linguistics and English aptly explained in their amicus
brief in Heller:

3
Under longstanding linguistic principles that
were well understood and recognized at the
time that the Second Amendment was adopted,
the “well regulated Militia” clause necessarily
adds meaning to the “keep and bear Arms”
clause by furnishing the reason for the latter’s
existence….On its face, the language of the
Amendment tells us that the reason why the
right of the people to keep and bear arms shall
not be infringed is because a well regulated
militia is necessary to the security of a free
state. The purpose of the Second Amendment,
therefore, is to perpetuate “a well regulated
militia.”
Brief for Professors of Linguistics & English, et al.  in
Heller, at 2-3 (Jan. 11, 2008) (the “Linguists’ Brief”).
The Heller majority acknowledged the term, “the
people,” was used in a collective sense throughout the
Bill of Rights and that “the militia” in colonial America
consisted of a subset of “the people,”  but the majority
concluded:
Reading the Second Amendment as protecting
only the right to “keep and bear Arms” in an
organized militia therefore fits poorly with the
operative clause’s description of the holder of
that right as “the people.” We start therefore
with a strong presumption that the Second
Amendment right is exercised individually and
belongs to all Americans.
Heller, 554 U.S. at 579-81.

4
We do not see the logic in this presumption. Reading
the Second Amendment as conferring a collective right for
the people of the states to maintain well regulated militias
fits perfectly with the Heller majority’s own previous
acknowledgements that “the people” refers to “a class of
persons who are part of a national community,” and that
“the militia” consists of “a subset of ‘the people.’” Heller,
554 U.S. at 580.
We also fail to see the logic in another statement in
which the Heller majority referred to the first half of the
Second Amendment as “The prefatory clause” and an
alleged right to private gun ownership as “the ancient
right:”
The prefatory clause does not suggest that
preserving the militia was the only reason
Americans valued the ancient right; most
undoubtedly thought it even more important
for self-defense and hunting.
Heller, 554 U.S. at 599.
The Heller majority presented no basis to support
its claim that “most” Americans “undoubtedly” believed
that private gun ownership was more important for selfdefense and hunting than to perpetuate a “well regulated
Militia,” nor did the majority provide any rationale for why,
if this claim were true, the Founders would have neglected
to even mention these other reasons in the first half of
the Second Amendment. See Heller, 554 U.S. at 599-600.
Moreover, as we discuss below, private gun ownership was
not an “ancient right,” nor does it confer any net defensive
benefit in a democratic society. See ibid.

5
Ultimately, Heller effectively deleted the first half
of the Second Amendment from the U.S. Constitution –
just as the National Rifle Association did in the version
of the Amendment that is inscribed on the wall of its
headquarters in Fairfax, Virginia. Michael Waldman,
How the NRA Rewrote the Second Amendment , Politico
(May 19, 2014).2
B. Heller is incompatible with the “keep and bear
Arms” clause.
The Heller majority opinion stated that the term “bear
arms” in the Second Amendment “in no way connotes
participation in a structured military organization.”
Heller, 554 U.S. at 584. But citing the Linguists’ Brief, the
Heller majority contradicted this claim by acknowledging,
“The phrase, ‘bear arms,’ also had at the time an idiomatic
meaning.” Id. at 586. The relevant portion of the Linguists’
Brief states:
The term “bear arms” is an idiom that means to
serve as a soldier, do military service, fight….
The word “arms” itself has an overwhelmingly
military meaning, referring to weapons of
offense or armor of defense.
Linguists Brief at 4. Yet in the next paragraph, the
Heller  majority claimed that applying the Linguists’
interpretation of “bear arms” in the Second Amendment
creates “an absurdity that no commentator has ever
endorsed.” Ibid. The majority went on to state:
2.  Available at https://www.politico.com/magazine/
story/2014/05/nra-guns-second-amendment-106856/  (last accessed
Oct. 24, 2026).

6
Worse still, the phrase “keep and bear Arms”
would be incoherent. The word “Arms” would
have two different meanings at once: “weapons”
(as the object of “keep”) and (as the object
of “bear”) one-half of an idiom. It would be
rather like saying “He filled and kicked the
bucket” to mean “He filled the bucket and died.”
Grotesque.
Id. at 587.
However, giving “bear arms” the idiomatic meaning
endorsed in the Linguists’ Brief is precisely the
interpretation of the “keep and bear Arms” clause that
the history and text of the Second Amendment indicate
the Founders intended. James Madison, who wrote the
original draft of what would eventually become the Second
Amendment, made it clear that he was using the term,
“bear arms,” to refer to carrying weapons in the setting
of military service for the common defense. Madison’s
original draft read:
The right of the people to keep and bear arms
shall not be infringed; a well armed and well
regulated militia being the best security
of a free country: but no person religiously
scrupulous of bearing arms, shall be compelled
to render military service in person.
1789 Annals of Congress, House of Representatives, at
451 (1789) (Joseph Gales ed. 1834).3
3.  Available at https://www.congress.gov/annals-of-congress/
volume-1.pdf (last accessed Oct. 24, 2026).

7
In Aymette v. State , 21 Tenn. 154, 159 (1840), the
Tennessee Supreme Court derided the claim that the
idiom, “bear arms,” referred to using guns for hunting
or self-defense, stating:
A man in the pursuit of deer, elk, and buffaloes
might carry his rifle every day for forty years,
and yet it would never be said of him that he
had borne arms; much less could it be said that
a private citizen bears arms because he had a
dirk or pistol concealed under his clothes, or a
spear in a cane.
In the interval between Heller and New York State
Rifle Association v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1 (2022), as Justice
Breyer noted in his dissent in Bruen , overwhelming
evidence was amassed, including searches of databases
compiled by Brigham Young University that include 40,000
texts documenting that the term, “keep and bear arms,”
was almost uniformly understood during the Founding
Era to refer to possessing and carrying weapons of war in
the setting of military service. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 109-110
(Breyer J., dissenting); Dennis Barron, Corpus Evidence
Illuminates the Meaning of Bear Arms , 46 Hastings
Const. L. Q. 509, 509-22 (2019).
C. The Second Amendment did not codify a broad
right to private gun ownership inherited from
English ancestors.
The Heller majority repeatedly referenced the 1689
English Declaration of Rights in claiming that the Second
Amendment codified a broad individual right to own
firearms that the Founders inherited from their English
ancestors. Heller, 554 U.S. at 582, 593-94, 605-06, 612-
13. The majority referred to “St. George Tucker” as an

8
important founding-era legal scholar (id. at 666 n. 32) and
quoted Tucker as writing that the Second Amendment
was the “true palladium of liberty.” Id. at 606. In the
same paragraph, though, Tucker also wrote that the
gun-related provision in the 1689 English Declaration of
Rights was so limited that “not one man in five hundred
can keep a gun in his house without being subject to a
penalty.” St. George Tucker, Blackstone’s Commentaries:
With Notes of Reference to the Constitution and Laws of
the Federal Government of the United States and of the
Commonwealth of Virginia , at 300 (1803).
The most obvious contemporary evidence that the
Founders could not possibly have inherited a broad right
to private gun ownership from their English ancestors
lies in the fact that although the 1689 English Declaration
of Rights has never been repealed, Britain currently
has some of the most stringent gun control laws of any
high income democratic country in the world, including
a complete ban on civilian ownership of handguns and
most automatic and semi-automatic long guns. Michael J.
North, Gun Control in Great Britain after the Dunblane
Shootings, Reducing Gun Violence in America: Informing
Policy with Evidence and Analysis 186-191 (Johns
Hopkins University Press 2013). In the words of Bob
Marshall-Andrews, a former member of Parliament who
participated in the debates during the enactment of the
handgun ban, the claim that the 1689 English Declaration
of Rights conferred a general right to firearm ownership
is “preposterous.” Bob Marshall-Andrews, Letter from
Bob Marshall-Andrews, QC, to Dr. Michael North , July
29 (2021).4
4.  Available at https://aagunv.org/wp-content/uploads/
2026/10/Letter-from-Bob-Marshall-Andrews.pdf  (last accessed
Oct. 24, 2026).

9
D. Heller violates stare decisis.
Before Heller, no United States gun control law had
ever been overturned by a federal court on the basis
that it violated the Second Amendment. As Justice
Stevens wrote in his dissent in Heller, “[F]or most of
our history, the invalidity of Second-Amendment-based
objections to firearms regulations has been well settled
and uncontroversial.” Heller, 554 U.S. at 676 (Stevens,
J., dissenting). As we document below, the retort by the
Heller majority, “For most of our history the question did
not present itself,” is plainly wrong. Id. at 626.
1. Pre- Heller cases directly related to the
Second Amendment.
a. United States v. Cruikshank, 92 U.S.
542 (1876).
Cruikshank  w as  th e  firs t  cas e  in  w hi c h  this  C o urt
ruled directly on the right conferred by the Second
Amendment. Based on the prevailing legal theory that
the Bill of Rights did not confer rights but only prevented
the federal government from infringing on rights derived
from other sources, the Court held that “bearing arms
for a lawful purpose” is “not a right granted by the
Constitution.” Cruikshank , 92 U.S. at 553. The Heller
majority stated:
The limited discussion of the Second Amendment
in Cruikshank  supports, if anything, the
individual-rights interpretation. There was
no claim in Cruikshank that the victims had
been deprived of their right to carry arms in
a militia.

10
Heller, 554 U.S. at 620. However, the persons whose
Second Amendment rights were in question in Cruikshank
were approximately 100 freed slaves who, after being
deputized by a local sheriff to bring their own weapons
to guard the courthouse in Colfax, Louisiana after a
disputed gubernatorial election, were murdered by the Ku
Klux Klan. Charles Lane, The Day Freedom Died: The
Colfax Massacre, the Supreme Court, and the Betrayal of
Reconstruction , 71-2 (Henry Holt & Co. 2008). The freed
slaves fit the Heller majority’s own definition of a “militia.”
b. Presser v. Illinois, 116 U.S. 255 (1886).
The Heller majority claimed Presser “does not refute
the individual-rights interpretation of the Amendment,”
and that “ Presser  said nothing about the Second
Amendment›s meaning or scope, beyond the fact that it
does not prevent the prohibition of private paramilitary
organizations.” Heller, 554 U.S. at 621. However, in his
dissent, Justice Stevens disputed this claim, citing the
following statement in Presser as evidence that the Court
interpreted the Second Amendment right as being related
to militia service:
The plaintiff in error was not a member of
the organized volunteer militia of the State of
Illinois, nor did he belong to the troops of the
United States or to any organization under
the militia law of the United States. On the
contrary, the fact that he did not belong to the
organized militia or the troops of the United
States was an ingredient in the offence for
which he was convicted and sentenced.

11
Id. at 673-74 (Stevens, J., dissenting) (quoting Presser,
116 U.S. at 266).
The Heller majority responded:
Unfortunately for Justice STEVENS’
argument, that later portion deals with
the  Fourteenth Amendment;  it  w a s
the  Fourteenth Amendment  to which the
plaintiff›s nonmembership in the militia was
relevant.
Heller, 554 U.S. at 621.
The Heller majority must have realized that the
Presser Court was commenting in this section on what
the nature of the Second Amendment right was that the
Fourteenth Amendment incorporated into a right enjoyed
by Hermann Presser.
c. United States v. Miller , 307 U.S. 174
(1939).
The Court ruled unanimously in Miller that the
National Firearms Act, which established registration
and tax requirements for private ownership of firearms
such as machine guns and short-barreled shotguns, did
not violate the Second Amendment. After quoting the full
Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution that describes the
power of Congress “To provide for organizing, arming,
and disciplining the Militia, and for governing such Part
of them as may be employed in the Service of the United
States,” the Court concluded:

12
With obvious purpose to assure the continuation
and render possible the effectiveness of such
forces the declaration and guarantee of the
Second Amendment were made. It must be
interpreted and applied with that end in view.
Miller, 307 U.S. at 178.
The ruling in Heller that the Second Amendment
protects an individual right to possess a firearm
unconnected with service in a well regulated militia
plainly conflicts with Miller.
As Justice Stevens observed in his dissenting opinion
in Heller, the Supreme Court’s unanimous ruling in
Miller stood as the definitive interpretation of the Second
Amendment from 1939 until the Heller decision in 2008:
The view of the Amendment we took in Miller
– that it protects the right to keep and bear
arms for certain military purposes, but that
it does not curtail the Legislature’s power to
regulate the nonmilitary use and ownership of
weapons – is both the most natural reading of
the Amendment’s text and the interpretation
most faithful to the history of its adoption.
Heller, 554 U.S. at 637-38 (Stevens, J., dissenting).
The Heller majority seized upon an aside in the Miller
decision in which the Court commented that the shortbarreled shotgun that Jack Miller and his accomplice were
convicted of carrying in violation of the NFA was not “any
part of the ordinary military equipment,” nor could “its

13
use could contribute to the common defense.” Heller, 554
U.S. at 622. The majority stated, “Beyond that, the opinion
provided no explanation of the content of the right.” Ibid.
But as we’ve documented above, this is untrue.
The Court went on to state:
We may as well consider at this point,
(for we will have to consider eventually)
what types of weapons Miller permits.  Read
in isolation, Miller’s phrase “part of ordinary
military equipment” could mean that only
those weapons useful in warfare are protected.
That would be a startling reading of the
opinion, since it would mean that the National
Firearms Act’s restrictions on machineguns (not
challenged in Miller) might be unconstitutional,
machineguns being useful in warfare in 1939.
Heller, 554 U.S. at 624.
The “startling” reading to which the Heller majority
referred is the logical consequence of the Heller majority’s
own interpretation of Miller. The majority attempted to
escape the trap it set for itself by claiming, “ Miller said,
as we have explained, that the sorts of weapons protected
were those “in common use at the time.” Heller, 554 U.S.
at 627. But the section of Miller decision that the Heller
majority referred to in support of this claim described the
types of weapons that civilians were required to furnish
for themselves at their own expense and bring with them
when they were called by the government into militia
service, not a constitutional right of civilians to own or
carry such weapons for any other purpose. Miller, 307
U.S. at 177-82.

14
Being unable to reconcile its ruling with Miller, the
Heller majority sought to undermine the credibility of the
Miller decision, claiming:
As for the text of the Court’s opinion itself, that
discusses none of the history of the Second
Amendment… Not a word (not a word)  about
the history of the Second Amendment. This is
the mighty rock upon which the dissent rests
its case.
Heller, 554 U.S. at 624. Justice Stevens’ dissent explained
why this was incorrect:
The majority cannot seriously believe that
the Miller Court did not consider any relevant
evidence; the majority simply does not approve
of the conclusion the Miller Court reached on
that evidence.
Id. at 679 (Stevens, J., dissenting).
2. Additional cases in the interval between
Miller and Heller.
Between 1939 and 2008, the Supreme Court commented
on the scope of the Second Amendment in Adams v.
Williams, 407 U.S. 143 (1972), and Lewis v. United States
445 U.S. 55 (1980), both involving convictions for illegal
possession of handguns, but in which attorneys for the
petitioners didn’t advance Second Amendment defenses
– probably because they realized that in the aftermath of
Miller, such defenses were likely to fail.

15
In Adams , Justice Douglas dissented from the
majority on the question of whether the respondent had
been subjected to unreasonable search and seizure, but
went out of his way to state:
A powerful lobby dins into the ears of our
citizenry that these gun purchases are

and deeply damaging.” Dobbs , 597 U.S. at 268.  It is
undeniable that the Heller decision and its progeny are
“deeply damaging.” In creating constitutional obstacles,
where none previously existed, to the adoption of stringent
gun control laws in the United States comparable to the
laws in other high income democratic countries, the Heller
decision and its progeny are literally death sentences for
tens of thousands of Americans annually. In overturning
Roe, the majority on this Court also stated, “We have
long recognized, however, that stare decisis  is ‘not an
inexorable command.’” Id. at 292. Applying the same
reasoning, the Heller decision, which itself violated the
principle of stare decisis, should not be considered “an
inexorable command.”

36
CONCLUSION
If this Court adheres to the history and text of the
Second Amendment and to its own stated principles,
it should not only conclude that banning U.S. civilians
from possessing AR-15’s does not violate the Second
Amendment; this Court should also acknowledge that the
Heller decision and its progeny were wrongly decided.
